newsitem.title: UK: Underdog Major, favourite Blair fight for UK votes.
newsitem.headline: Underdog Major, favourite Blair fight for UK votes.

text.p: Fighting to avoid a widely forecast election defeat, Prime Minister John Major warned voters on Wednesday that the economic transformation of Britain achieved by his Conservatives was "too good to give up".

As party leaders set out to court the country's 44 million voters in the final 24 hours of campaigning, Major dismissed polls giving Labour a 20-point lead, saying: "I don't share the opinion...that we're going to lose tomorrow.
"I think this election is there to be won," he told BBC radio. "There are huge numbers of people who are undecided."
Labour Party leader Tony Blair, whose party last won an election in 1974, also dismissed polls predicting an opposition landslide when polling booths close on Thursday evening (2100 GMT).

Blair, who calls himself the "eternal warrior against complacency", told cheering supporters in Scotland: "I ask you here, here in Dumfries in Scotland and throughout the whole of Britain, come, join us, support us."
Blair has revitalised Labour since becoming leader in July 1994 by dragging it from the left to the political centre.
He was in Dumfries as part of a final campaign dash after an early-morning London news conference where he said: "We will not stop trying to persuade people to put their trust in Labour.
"Between now and when the polls close tomorrow night we will strive for every vote, in every corner of the country."
A leading firm of bookmakers said it had stopped taking bets on Labour gaining the most seats at the May 1 election.
William Hill said it took the decision after the odds on Labour winning most seats fell to just 1-12, the point where punters would pay more in tax than they would get in winnings.

The last time the firm closed its books on an election was in 1979 when the Conservatives swept to power under Margaret Thatcher and began 18 years of one-party rule -- the longest unbroken stretch this century.
Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke broke the unwritten rule of not mentioning defeat, warning the ruling party against tearing itself apart after a Labour victory.

Clarke, who has fought a rearguard action from within the cabinet to slow the party's drift to a more right-wing, anti-European stance, told Sky News: "I think the people who turn afterwards to post mortems and scapegoating will make us look ridiculous.

"I have been in parties which have lost elections and the thing to do is pick yourself up and work out how you are going to win the next one and that is not by having internecine warfare and recriminations."
Labour's huge opinion poll lead has been steady for two years and has held up since Major called the election on March 17, hoping to wear Labour down with the longest campaign for more than 80 years.
No party has ever come back from such a deficit to win.

Major pulled off a surprise victory almost single-handedly in 1992 but a Conservative win on Thursday would arguably be the biggest political sensation since 1945, when voters threw out war-time prime minister Winston Churchill in a Labour landslide.
This time Labour needs a vote swing of 4.3 percent from the Conservatives over 1992 figures to win an overall majority.

The 20-point lead shown by current polls would give Labour a majority of around 200 seats. But no one is expecting that size of victory and the overall picture is complicated by Britain's first-past-the-post electoral system.

Support for the minority Liberal Democrats is also firm at around 15 percent compared to Labour's 50 and the Conservatives 30 percent. The Liberal Democrats could hold the balance of power if neither Labour nor the Conservatives gain a majority.
They are expected to support Labour in such a scenario, with radical reform of the voting system the price for cooperation.
